content: Two primary methods are commonly employed in formative assessments: key-informant interviews and focus groups. Additional participatory techniques, such as free listing and pile sorting, can be utilized to refine the language used in survey questions, informed consent forms, and transitional text within surveys. Mapping and ranking exercises are also valuable tools in this context. For further details on qualitative methods, including the development of interview guides and data analysis, refer to Chapter A-12. The data collected during formative assessments can significantly inform all aspects of the development of Behavioral and Biological Surveillance (BBS) protocols. It is essential to review the findings of the BBS in conjunction with the results of the formative assessment to ensure accurate interpretation. Moreover, formative data can enhance service provision and policymaking. For instance, service providers may believe they are adequately serving men who have sex with men (MSM), but if MSM cannot identify a single organization targeting their needs, this disconnect must be addressed. This gap highlights the need to engage MSM in identifying necessary services and their delivery. Investigators should begin developing the BBS protocol as soon as the formative assessment identifies the most suitable recruitment method. Concurrently, findings from the formative assessment should be disseminated through a report and presented to key stakeholders. Ideally, formative assessment should be an ongoing process throughout the BBS. Investigators must regularly consult the target population to identify potential issues that could impact participation or survey execution. For example, law enforcement may begin targeting the population with arrests, or reimbursement for participation may be insufficient to recruit an adequate sample size. Conversely, excessive reimbursement may incentivize ineligible individuals to falsely claim membership in the target population. This consultation can involve conducting exit interviews with survey participants, providing an anonymous suggestion box for feedback, or engaging in discussions with stakeholders, including community-based organization staff who work with the target population. Exit interviews and their associated questions should be incorporated into the formative assessment protocol. Findings from ongoing formative assessments can be used to revise and strengthen survey procedures. Standardized instruments for collecting survey data among key populations—such as MSM, people who inject drugs (PWID), sex workers (SW), and transgender persons (TG)—are provided in the questionnaire module section of these guidelines. These instruments have been field-tested and, where applicable, include validated questions and scoring systems. Investigators are strongly encouraged to use these established questionnaires for two main reasons. First, questionnaire development is a complex process requiring extensive preparatory work, including cognitive testing and evaluation. The provided instruments include tested questions, time references, and skip patterns known to yield high-quality data. Second, these instruments contain questions that have been used globally, enabling researchers to compare survey results across countries. The standardized instruments are designed for self-administration using electronic data-collection methods, such as tablets, laptops, or smartphones, but can be adapted for paper-based data collection if necessary. When planning a survey, investigators should understand the advantages and disadvantages of various data-collection methods to select the most appropriate approach for the circumstances. Key steps in questionnaire development include deciding on the method of administration, determining investigation topics, and pilot testing the survey tool. The questionnaire may be delivered by an interviewer or self-administered by participants. For self-administered interviews, questions and instructions must be clear and leave no room for misunderstanding, as participants may not feel comfortable seeking clarification. Misunderstanding questions can lead to invalid responses. Data collection can be conducted using paper-based or electronic methods. Paper-based questionnaires require additional time for interviewer training and may necessitate prior experience with complex surveys. Participants completing self-administered paper-based questionnaires must be moderately literate and able to follow instructions. The number and complexity of skip instructions should be minimized, especially for self-administered questionnaires. Data from paper-based surveys can be entered electronically shortly after the interview or later in batches, with double data entry strongly recommended to minimize errors. Electronic data collection instruments can also be interviewer-administered or self-administered. These instruments can be developed using various software platforms, such as the Questionnaire Development System (QDS™) or Open Data Kit (ODK). Electronic data collection offers advantages such as eliminating the need for subsequent data entry, ensuring consistent questionnaire delivery, and allowing for immediate clarification of questions and responses. However, electronic methods may require additional resources and technical expertise. When developing or adapting a questionnaire, investigators must consider several factors, including the choice of variables, recall period, question order, and interview length. The data collected should be essential for understanding the target population and responding to the epidemic. Recall periods should balance the risk of recall bias with the ability to measure specific behaviors. Questionnaires should begin with easy, salient, and non-threatening questions, progressing from general to specific topics. Transitional phrases should be used when changing topics to help participants adjust their thinking. The questionnaire should be as concise as possible, removing redundant or unnecessary questions to minimize participant fatigue and improve data quality. All BBS surveys should collect standard information on demographics, risk behaviors, and access to HIV testing, prevention, and healthcare services. Additional domains may include sexual and reproductive health, mental health, psychosocial support, stigma and discrimination, and knowledge of HIV prevention and transmission. These domains can be tailored to the target population, survey context, and information needs. Pretesting the questionnaire is crucial to determine the time participants are willing to devote to the interview and to adjust the length accordingly.
